concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: This is the named research subject and defines the transfer of WAL content into the database.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpoint configuration
concepts.reason: Thresholds and callbacks determine when SQLite initiates checkpoints automatically.

concepts.name: PASSIVE checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: PASSIVE defines checkpoint behavior without waiting for readers or writers.

concepts.name: FULL checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: FULL defines waiting conditions and completion behavior for checkpointing all frames.

concepts.name: RESTART checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: RESTART adds reader waiting that permits the next writer to restart the WAL.

concepts.name: TRUNCATE checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: TRUNCATE extends RESTART by reducing the WAL file to zero bytes.

concepts.name: NOOP checkpoint mode
concepts.reason: NOOP provides checkpoint status without checkpointing frames.

concepts.name: Checkpoint locking
concepts.reason: Checkpoint and writer locks govern concurrent checkpoint execution.

concepts.name: Busy-handler fallback
concepts.reason: Busy-handler refusal changes blocking checkpoints into partial nonblocking work.

concepts.name: Checkpoint status counters
concepts.reason: Output counters report WAL frames and cumulative checkpoint progress.

concepts.name: Checkpoint database targeting
concepts.reason: The database argument controls whether checkpointing targets one or all attached WAL databases.

concepts.name: Checkpoint synchronization ordering
concepts.reason: Storage synchronization ordering is part of safe checkpoint execution.

concepts.name: Checkpoint starvation
concepts.reason: Persistent reader overlap can prevent checkpoint completion and WAL reset.

concepts.name: WAL recycling after checkpointing
concepts.reason: Completed checkpointing enables WAL reuse under specified reader and synchronization conditions.

concepts.name: Checkpoint scheduling and performance
concepts.reason: Checkpoint placement and frequency affect commit latency and read performance.

concepts.name: Checkpoint progress and reader end marks
concepts.reason: Reader end marks limit checkpoint progress and determine where later invocations resume.

concepts.name: SQLite write-ahead logging
concepts.reason: The broader WAL mechanism supplies context but exceeds the named checkpointing scope.

concepts.name: Rollback journaling
concepts.reason: Rollback journaling is a separate journaling approach rather than an internal checkpointing concept.

claims.text: A checkpoint moves transactions from the WAL file back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers automatic checkpointing after a commit when the WAL contains at least N frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing N equal to zero or a negative value to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Registering a callback with sqlite3_wal_hook disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: Each new database connection enables automatic checkpointing with a default threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT value.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint are PASSIVE.
claims.quote: The wal_autocheckpoint pragma can be used to invoke this interface from SQL. Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE .

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits through the busy handler until no database writer exists and all readers use the most recent database snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: After satisfying its waiting conditions, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL checkpoints every log frame and syncs the database file.
claims.quote: It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: While SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL is pending, it blocks new writers but permits new readers to continue unimpeded.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART performs FULL behavior and then waits through the busy handler until all readers read only from the database file.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only.

claims.text: Successful SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART completion ensures that the next writer restarts the log from its beginning.
claims.quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE performs RESTART behavior and additionally truncates the log to zero bytes immediately before a successful return.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP checkpoints zero frames and serves to retrieve the pnLog and pnCkpt output values.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: If another checkpoint prevents acquisition of the exclusive checkpoint lock, the call returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE also acquire an exclusive writer lock.
claims.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero while acquiring the writer lock or waiting for readers, the checkpoint continues with PASSIVE behavior and returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: When pnLog is non-NULL, it receives the total log-frame count, or -1 if an error or non-WAL database prevents checkpoint execution.
claims.quote: *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL mode

claims.text: The pnCkpt count includes frames checkpointed before the current call.
claims.quote: the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: After a successful SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE, both pnLog and pnCkpt are zero.
claims.quote: upon successful completion of an SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE, the log file will have been truncated to zero bytes and so both *pnLog and *pnCkpt will be set to zero.

claims.text: A NULL or empty zDb requests the operation on every attached WAL database.
claims.quote: If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db.

claims.text: When zDb is NULL or empty, pnLog and pnCkpt output values are undefined.
claims.quote: In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: For a named attached database outside WAL mode, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 returns SQLITE_OK and sets both counters to -1.
claims.quote: If database zDb is the name of an attached database that is not in WAL mode, SQLITE_OK is returned and both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.

claims.text: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before its content moves into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: The database file must be synced before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL. Checkpoint also requires more seeking.

claims.text: If overlapping readers always leave at least one reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Reader gaps avoid the described starvation scenario when checkpoints are attempted during periods with no readers.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: A write transaction prevents WAL reset until that transaction ends.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.

claims.text: During a write, the writer rewinds the WAL when all WAL content has been transferred and synced and no reader uses the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: Checkpointing normally recycles the existing WAL without truncating it, with journal_size_limit identified as an exception.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: By default, the thread whose COMMIT pushes the WAL over its size limit runs the automatic checkpoint.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: A COMMIT that triggers checkpointing can be much slower than ordinary COMMIT operations.
claims.quote: This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claims.text: Increasing WAL size degrades read performance despite the wal-index.
claims.quote: The wal-index helps find content in the WAL file much faster, but performance still falls off with increasing WAL file size.

claims.text: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers but must stop before passing any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: The checkpoint records progress in the wal-index and resumes from that position on its next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

limitations: All three sources originate from SQLite; they provide primary authority but do not meet an independent-origin source floor.
S2's dedicated API reference governs mode semantics over S1's narrower three-mode overview and its inconsistent reference to RESET.

S1 says RESTART and TRUNCATE might block readers, while S2 explicitly says RESTART does not impede readers and defines TRUNCATE as RESTART plus truncation; the mode claims follow S2, and the packet does not explain the discrepancy.

S1's broad wording about checkpoint completion requiring no other transactions must be distinguished from copying all frames: S2 permits FULL completion while readers use the most recent snapshot, whereas RESTART additionally waits for readers to use only the database file.
No independent corroboration, version-by-version mode history, or resolution of the source discrepancies is available in the supplied packet.
The single bounded extraction pass does not demonstrate research saturation; the new-information rate is the fraction of extracted claims newly added in that pass.
